questions.task: Install the httpd web server package using DNF and configure it to start automatically at boot.
questions.check: Run 'rpm -q httpd' to confirm the package is installed and 'systemctl is-enabled --quiet httpd' should return no output (exit status 0), indicating the service is enabled.

questions.task: Switch SELinux from enforcing to permissive mode and verify the change.
questions.check: Execute 'getenforce' – it should output 'Permissive'. Also, after a reboot, 'getenforce' should still show 'Permissive', confirming the persistent configuration.

questions.task: Configure a static IP address on the RHEL 9 VM that matches the NAT subnet used by VMware Workstation Player (e.g., 192.168.219.0/24).
steps: Determine the NAT subnet used by VMware (e.g., on the host run: cat /etc/vmware/vmnet8/nat/nat.conf | grep subnet). Assume it is 192.168.219.0/24 for this exercise.
Log in to the RHEL 9 VM as root or with sudo privileges.
Identify the network interface name (usually ens33 or eth0): ip link show
Create or edit the interface configuration file, e.g.: sudo vi /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-ens33
Add or modify the following lines in the file:
Restart the network service: sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager
Verify the new address: ip a show dev ens33
questions.check: The command `ip a` should display the interface with the address 192.168.219.100/24, and `ping -c 3 192.168.219.2` should succeed, confirming connectivity to the NAT gateway.

questions.task: Create a new VMware Workstation Player virtual machine named "server1" for RHEL 9, allocate a 20 GB virtual disk, and attach the RHEL 9 installation ISO.
steps: Choose **File → New Virtual Machine** to launch the New Virtual Machine Wizard.
Select **I will install the operating system later** and click **Next**.
For the guest operating system, choose **Linux** and then **Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 64-bit**, then click **Next**.
Enter **server1** as the virtual machine name and choose a location for the VM files, then click **Next**.
Set the virtual disk size to **20 GB**, select **Store virtual disk as a single file**, and click **Next**.
Click **Finish** to create the VM (it will appear in the player in a Powered Off state).
Select the newly created **server1** VM and click **Edit virtual machine settings**.
In the hardware list, select **CD/DVD (SATA)**, ensure **Connect at power on** is checked, then click **Browse** and locate the downloaded **RHEL-9.x.x-x86_64-dvd.iso** file.
Click **OK** to close the settings window.
With the VM still selected, click **Power on this virtual machine**.
questions.check: The virtual machine should power on and display the Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 installer screen, confirming that the VM was created with the correct OS type, disk size, and ISO attached.

questions.task: Navigate to your own home directory and the root user's home directory using the tilde (~) shortcut and verify you are in the correct locations.
steps: log in as a regular user (e.g., mj)
questions.check: The first pwd should output /home/mj and the second pwd should output /root. The ls ~ for the regular user should list files in /home/mj, while the ls ~ for root should display at least the file anaconda-ks.cfg.

questions.task: Demonstrate the use of absolute and relative paths by listing the contents of the /home directory from the root directory.
questions.check: Both ls commands should produce identical listings of the /home directory, confirming that "home" (relative) and "/home" (absolute) refer to the same location when the current directory is "/".

questions.task: Add a new regular user entry to /etc/passwd using vipw by copying the root line and editing the fields to create user "tweedle" with UID 1001, GID 1001, comment "Tweedle Dee", and home directory "/home/tweedle".
questions.check: grep '^tweedle:' /etc/passwd && awk -F: '$1=="tweedle" {print $3,$4,$5,$6}' /etc/passwd | grep -q '^1001 1001 Tweedle Dee /home/tweedle$'

questions.task: Edit /etc/shadow with vipw -s to create a matching shadow entry for the newly added user "tweedle" and verify the entry exists.
questions.check: grep '^tweedle:' /etc/shadow

questions.task: Create a new static Ethernet connection profile named "eth0-work" for interface eth0, configure its IP settings, bring it up, and verify the static address is in use.
steps: nmcli con add con-name "eth0-work" type ethernet ifname eth0
questions.check: The output of `ip addr show eth0` must contain the line `inet 192.168.20.100/24` and `ip route` must show a default route via `192.168.20.1`.

questions.task: Back up the current NetworkManager connection file for eth0, change the connection to use DHCP via the text UI (nmtui), and confirm the change with a diff and nmcli output.
steps: CON_NAME=$(nmcli -g name con show | grep -i eth0 | head -n1)
# In the nmtui interface: select "Edit a connection", choose the $CON_NAME entry, set "IPv4 CONFIGURATION" to "Automatic (DHCP)", press <OK>, then <Back>, and finally <Quit>.
questions.check: The `diff` command must show changes in the file where `ipv4.method=auto` replaces a previous static setting, and `nmcli con show "$CON_NAME"` must display `ipv4.method: auto`. Additionally, `ip addr show eth0` should now show an address obtained from DHCP rather than the previous static address.

questions.task: Uninstall a package and verify that a modified configuration file is saved with a .rpmsave extension
steps: echo "# Test comment added by RHCSA practice" | sudo tee -a /etc/wgetrc
questions.check: The file /etc/wgetrc.rpmsave should exist (showing the original configuration saved) and "rpm -q wget" should report that the package is not installed.

questions.task: Install an RPM directly from a remote URL using rpm and confirm the installation
questions.check: The command "rpm -q fortune-mod" should output the package name and version, indicating the package was successfully installed from the remote location.

questions.task: List all available module streams on the system.
questions.check: The command output displays a table with a "Name" column containing entries such as "nodejs" and a "Stream" column showing versions like "18".

questions.task: Install the Node.js 18 module stream (default profile) and verify the installed version.
questions.check: The output of `node -v` starts with "v18." indicating that Node.js version 18 is installed.

questions.task: Show the backward‑compatible runlevel target links and verify which systemd targets they point to
questions.check: The command lists files runlevel0.target … runlevel6.target, each as a symbolic link; for example, runlevel0.target → poweroff.target, runlevel1.target → rescue.target, runlevel3.target → multi-user.target, runlevel5.target → graphical.target, etc.

questions.task: Display all units that are pulled in when the graphical target starts
questions.check: The output shows a tree of units required by graphical.target, including display‑manager.service, network.target, sound.target, and other services that constitute a full graphical multi‑user system.

questions.task: Create a regular user and verify that it receives a UID/GID in the normal user range, gets a home directory, and is assigned a private group with the same ID as the user.
questions.check: The grep of USERGROUPS_ENAB should show 'yes'. The /etc/passwd line for alice must have a UID between 1000 and 60000. The directory /home/alice must exist, be owned by alice:alice, and have permissions 700 (default). The primary group name returned by 'id -gn alice' must be the same as the username, and the numeric GID returned by 'id -g alice' must equal the UID returned by 'id -u alice'.

questions.task: Create a system account using the -r option and confirm that it receives a UID/GID in the system range and does not get a home directory.
questions.check: The SYS_UID_MIN and SYS_UID_MAX lines should show values 201 and 999. The /etc/passwd entry for sysacct must have a UID between 201 and 999. The test for /home/sysacct should report "No home" (i.e., the directory does not exist). The UID and GID reported by id must both be within the 201‑999 range, and the group entry retrieved by getent must exist.

questions.task: Provide default files for new users by copying /usr/share/doc/bash into /etc/skel and verify that a newly created user receives those files in their home directory.
questions.check: The directory /home/infouser/bash (and its contents) exists and is identical to /usr/share/doc/bash; you can confirm with: diff -r /usr/share/doc/bash /home/infouser/bash

questions.task: Lock a user account, verify the lock in /etc/shadow, then unlock it and set an expiration date of 2000-01-01.
questions.check: After the lock step, the password field for testlock in /etc/shadow starts with an exclamation mark (!). After unlocking, the exclamation mark is removed. The final grep shows the 8th field (expiration) set to the numeric value representing 2000-01-01 (e.g., 9497).

questions.task: Verify that the /bin directory is a symbolic link to /usr/bin on RHEL 9.
questions.check: The first command shows that /bin is a symlink (e.g., "lrwxrwxrwx ... /bin -> /usr/bin"). The second command outputs "/usr/bin", confirming the link target.

questions.task: Create a 20 MiB file, format it as ext4, and mount it on /mnt to practise using the /mnt mount point.
questions.check: The df output shows a filesystem of about 20 MiB mounted on /mnt/tmpmount, confirming the mount succeeded.

questions.task: List all configured partitions on the system.
questions.check: The command output displays a table of partitions for each attached disk (e.g., /dev/sda, /dev/sdb) confirming that fdisk listed all partitions.

questions.task: Create an XFS filesystem on /dev/sdb3, mount it at /mnt/data, and make the mount persistent via /etc/fstab.
questions.check: The directory /mnt/data is a mount point (mountpoint -q /mnt/data) and `df -T | grep /mnt/data` shows the filesystem type as xfs. Additionally, `grep /dev/sdb3 /etc/fstab` confirms the entry was added.

questions.task: Disable a SELinux boolean temporarily, then enable it permanently so the change survives a reboot, and verify each state.
questions.check: The first getsebool after the temporary change should show 'httpd_enable_cgi --> off'. After the -P command, getsebool should show 'httpd_enable_cgi --> on', and the setting will be stored in /etc/selinux/ (e.g., /etc/selinux/targeted/booleans.local), confirming it will persist across reboots.

questions.task: Display the SELinux context of a file, change its type to one appropriate for a web server, and confirm the new context is applied.
questions.check: The first ls -Z should show a default type such as 'default_t'. After chcon, the second ls -Z must display the type 'httpd_sys_content_t' for /tmp/webtest.txt, confirming the context change.

questions.task: Switch the system to the 'throughput-performance' tuned profile and verify that it is active, then restore the originally recommended profile.
steps: # if [ "$(tuned-adm active | awk '{print $NF}')" != "throughput-performance" ]; then echo "Profile not active"; exit 1; fi
questions.check: The output of the first 'tuned-adm active' command should contain 'throughput-performance'. After restoring, the final 'tuned-adm active' output should match the profile saved in /tmp/original_profile.txt.

questions.task: Create a gzip‑compressed tar archive of the /etc directory, verify the archive, and extract it to /tmp/etc‑backup.
questions.check: The archive file /tmp/etc_backup.tar.gz must exist and be non‑empty. The file counts before and after extraction should be identical (diff returns no differences), confirming a successful archive and extraction.

questions.task: Enable persistent systemd journal storage and verify that logs survive a reboot
questions.check: The directory /var/log/journal exists and contains binary journal files, and after the reboot 'journalctl -b -1' displays log entries from the previous boot, confirming persistence.

questions.task: Compare reading the binary lastlog file directly with using the lastlog command
questions.check: The 'cat' (or hexdump) output is unreadable binary data, while the 'lastlog' command prints a readable table of users and their last login times. The man page confirms that lastlog reads from /var/log/lastlog.

questions.task: Build a Python web server container image and run it, exposing it on host port 8000.
steps: echo "Welcome to our simple webserver!" > index.html

cat > Containerfile <<'EOF'
FROM python:3-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY index.html /app/
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["python", "-m", "http.server", "8000"]
EOF
questions.check: The 'podman images' output lists an image named 'python-webserver', 'podman ps' shows a container named 'simple-webserver' with status 'Up', and the curl command returns the exact text 'Welcome to our simple webserver!'.

questions.task: Stop the running simple-webserver container.
questions.check: The container 'simple-webserver' appears in 'podman ps -a' with a status of 'Exited' (or not listed in 'podman ps' without -a).

questions.task: Configure hostname, root password, register the system, install Apache, and set up a custom DocumentRoot on port 8234.
questions.check: hostname -f should output 'tester1.example.com'; 'su - root' should accept password 'changeme'; 'subscription-manager status' should show an attached subscription; 'ss -tlnp | grep 8234' should list httpd listening on 0.0.0.0:8234; 'curl http://localhost:8234' should return 'Success!'.

questions.task: Open firewall and add SELinux rules so the Apache service can serve content on the custom port 8234 and the /html directory.
steps: semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8234 || semanage port -m -t http_port_t -p tcp 8234
questions.check: firewall-cmd --list-ports should include '8234/tcp'; 'semanage port -l | grep 8234' should show type 'http_port_t'; 'ls -Zd /html' should display SELinux context 'httpd_sys_content_t'; 'curl http://localhost:8234' should still return 'Success!'.

questions.check: After a reboot, journalctl --list-boots lists more than one boot.

questions.task: Format /dev/vdb1 as XFS and mount it at /data, by UUID, so it survives a reboot.
steps: Add to /etc/fstab:  UUID=<the UUID>  /data  xfs  defaults  0 0
questions.check: findmnt /data shows it mounted. Running mount -a without errors proves the fstab line is valid, so the system won't stop at boot.

questions.check: swapon --show lists /dev/vdb2 at about 512M; free -h shows the extra swap.
